#### 3.5.3. Push Notification Delivery¶

Push notifications are delivered via HTTP POST to client-registered webhook endpoints. The delivery semantics and reliability guarantees are defined in Section 4.3.

### 3.6 Versioning¶

The specific version of the A2A protocol in use is identified using the `Major.Minor` elements (e.g. `1.0`) of the corresponding A2A specification version. Patch version numbers used by the specification, do not affect protocol compatibility. Patch version numbers SHOULD NOT be used in requests, responses and Agent Cards, and MUST not be considered when clients and servers negotiate protocol versions.

#### 3.6.1 Client Responsibilities¶

Clients MUST send the `A2A-Version` header with each request to maintain compatibility after an agent upgrades to a new version of the protocol (except for 0.3 Clients - 0.3 will be assumed for empty header). Sending the `A2A-Version` header also provides visibility to agents about version usage in the ecosystem, which can help inform the risks of inplace version upgrades.

Example of HTTP GET Request with Version Header:
    
    `GET /tasks/task-123 HTTP/1.1
    Host: agent.example.com
    A2A-Version: 1.0
    Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9...
    Accept: application/json
    `

Clients MAY provide the `A2A-Version` as a request parameter instead of a header.

Example of HTTP GET Request with Version request parameter:
    
    `GET /tasks/task-123?A2A-Version=1.0 HTTP/1.1
    Host: agent.example.com
    Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9...
    Accept: application/json
    `

#### 3.6.2 Server Responsibilities¶

Agents MUST process requests using the semantics of the requested `A2A-Version` (matching `Major.Minor`). If the version is not supported by the interface, agents MUST return a `VersionNotSupportedError`.

Agents MUST interpret empty value as 0.3 version.

Agents CAN expose multiple interfaces for the same transport with different versions under the same or different URLs.

#### 3.6.3 Tooling support¶

Tooling libraries and SDKs that implement the A2A protocol MUST provide mechanisms to help clients manage protocol versioning, such as negotiation of the transport and protocol version used. Client Agents that require the latest features of the protocol should be configured to request specific versions and avoid automatic fallback to older versions, to prevent silently losing functionality.

## 14. IANA Considerations¶

This section provides registration templates for the A2A protocol's media type, HTTP headers, and well-known URI, intended for submission to the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA).

### 14.1. Media Type Registration¶

#### 14.1.1. application/a2a+json¶

Type name: `application`

Subtype name: `a2a+json`

Required parameters: None

Optional parameters:

  * None

Encoding considerations: Binary (UTF-8 encoding MUST be used for JSON text)

Security considerations: This media type shares security considerations common to all JSON-based formats as described in RFC 8259, Section 12. Additionally:

  * Content MUST be validated against the A2A protocol schema before processing
  * Implementations MUST sanitize user-provided content to prevent injection attacks
  * File references within A2A messages MUST be validated to prevent server-side request forgery (SSRF)
  * Authentication and authorization MUST be enforced as specified in Section 7 of the A2A specification

Change controller: A2A Protocol Working Group

Provisional registration: No

### 14.2. HTTP Header Field Registrations¶

Note: The following HTTP headers represent the HTTP-based protocol binding implementation of the abstract A2A service parameters defined in Section 3.2.6. These registrations are specific to HTTP/HTTPS transports.

#### 14.2.1. A2A-Version Header¶

Header field name: A2A-Version

Applicable protocol: HTTP

Status: Standard

Author/Change controller: A2A Protocol Working Group

Specification document: Section 3.2.5 of the A2A Protocol Specification

Related information: The A2A-Version header field indicates the A2A protocol version that the client is using. The value MUST be in the format `Major.Minor` (e.g., "0.3"). If the version is not supported by the agent, the agent returns a `VersionNotSupportedError`.

Example:
    
    `A2A-Version: 0.3
    `

#### 14.2.2. A2A-Extensions Header¶

Header field name: A2A-Extensions

Applicable protocol: HTTP

Status: Standard

Author/Change controller: A2A Protocol Working Group

Specification document: Section 3.2.5 of the A2A Protocol Specification

Related information: The A2A-Extensions header field contains a comma-separated list of extension URIs that the client wants to use for the request. Extensions allow agents to provide additional functionality beyond the core A2A specification while maintaining backward compatibility.

Example:
    
    `A2A-Extensions: https://example.com/extensions/geolocation/v1,https://standards.org/extensions/citations/v1
    `

### 14.3. Well-Known URI Registration¶

URI suffix: agent-card.json

Change controller: A2A Protocol Working Group

Specification document: Section 8.2 of the A2A Protocol Specification

Related information: The `.well-known/agent-card.json` URI provides a standardized location for discovering an A2A agent's capabilities, supported protocols, authentication requirements, and available skills. The resource at this URI MUST return an AgentCard object as defined in Section 4.4.1 of the A2A specification.

Status: Permanent

Security considerations:

  * The Agent Card MAY contain public information about an agent's capabilities and SHOULD NOT include sensitive credentials or internal implementation details
  * Implementations SHOULD support HTTPS to ensure authenticity and integrity of the Agent Card
  * Agent Cards MAY be signed using JSON Web Signatures (JWS) as specified in the AgentCardSignature object (Section 4.4.7)
  * Clients SHOULD verify signatures when present to ensure the Agent Card has not been tampered with
  * Extended Agent Cards retrieved via authenticated endpoints (Section 3.1.11) MAY contain additional information and MUST enforce appropriate access controls

Example:
    
    `https://agent.example.com/.well-known/agent-card.json
    `

  * Both protocols are now projects of the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation: MCP since December 2025 (current revision 2026-07-28) and A2A as a Growth Stage project since August 2026 (current release v1.0.1).
  * Authentication differs in kind: MCP specifies a full OAuth 2.1 flow in which the MCP server is a resource server, while A2A lets each agent declare its schemes (API key, HTTP, OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect, mutual TLS) in its Agent Card and leaves credential acquisition out of band.
  * Most production systems that use A2A also use MCP: A2A carries work between agents, and each agent uses MCP to reach its own tools, so the real design question is where the boundary between agents sits.
  * Gateways now cover both sides: Bifrost, for example, filters MCP tools per virtual key and, since v2.3.0 on 13 October 2026, proxies A2A agents with per-key grants and logs that link agent tasks to the model and tool calls inside them.

The short answer to A2A vs MCP is that they solve different problems and most serious agent systems end up using both. Versioning  | Date-stamped revisions (`YYYY-MM-DD`)  | Semantic (`Major.Minor`; patch does not affect compatibility)
Current version  | 2026-07-28  | v1.0.1 (28 May 2026)
Previous version  | 2025-11-25  | v1.0.0 (12 March 2026); v0.3.0 (30 July 2025)
Version negotiation  | `io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion` in `_meta`, mirrored in the `MCP-Protocol-Version` header  | `A2A-Version` header on every request

Both projects shipped a breaking release in 2026. MCP’s 2026-07-28 changelog removed protocol-level sessions and the `initialize` handshake, so “every request now carries its protocol version and client capabilities”, added a mandatory `server/discover` call, moved long-running tasks into an official extension, and deprecated Roots, Sampling and Logging. A2A’s v1.0 notes renamed operations (`message/send` became `SendMessage`), changed enums to forms such as `TASK_STATE_COMPLETED`, removed the `kind` discriminator, and made `a2a.proto` the normative source for every binding. If you built against either protocol in 2025, plan a migration.
A2A was created by Google in April 2025, moved to the Linux Foundation in June 2025 and became a Growth Stage project of the Agentic AI Foundation on 27 August 2026.

What are the latest versions of MCP and A2A?

As of October 2026, the current MCP revision is 2026-07-28, which removed sessions and the initialize handshake. The latest A2A release is v1.0.1, tagged on 28 May 2026; v1.0.0 shipped on 12 March 2026.

How does authentication work in MCP compared with A2A?

In MCP, authorisation is optional, but HTTP servers that use it act as OAuth 2.1 resource servers, publish Protected Resource Metadata and must reject tokens not issued for them. In A2A, each agent lists its security schemes in its Agent Card, the client obtains credentials out of band and sends them in headers, and an agent can pause a task in an auth-required state.

Can I expose an A2A agent as an MCP tool instead?

You can wrap a narrowly scoped, stateless agent skill as an MCP tool or resource, and the A2A documentation allows for it. It loses what A2A adds: task state, multi-turn input, streaming updates, push notifications and an opaque boundary between organisations. Use the wrapper for simple lookups, not for long-running delegated work.

Do I need a gateway for A2A and MCP?

Not for a prototype. Once several teams share tool servers or agents, a gateway gives one place to decide which caller may reach which tool or agent, to hold upstream credentials and to log calls. Bifrost, LiteLLM and IBM's ContextForge all document A2A handling alongside MCP or model traffic.

### 3.7 Messages and Artifacts

Section titled “3.7 Messages and Artifacts”

Messages and Artifacts serve distinct purposes within the A2A protocol. The core interaction model defined by A2A is for clients to send messages to initiate a task that produces one or more artifacts.

Messages play several key roles:

  * Task Initiation: Clients send Messages to agents to initiate new tasks.
  * Clarification Messages: Agents may send Messages back to the client to request clarification prior to initiating a task.
  * Status Messages: Agents attach Messages to status update events to inform clients about task progress, request additional input, or provide informational updates.

## A2A in production​

A2A latest currently points to released version 1.0.0. It is an open protocol for communication between opaque agents, with a canonical protobuf data model and protocol bindings for JSON-RPC, gRPC, and HTTP+JSON/REST. Google created A2A, and the Linux Foundation announced the A2A project under its governance in June 2025.

### Agent Cards​

A2A discovery starts with an Agent Card. The recommended well-known URL is `https://{agent-server-domain}/.well-known/agent-card.json`, and the A2A IANA section registers `agent-card.json` as the well-known suffix. The card describes identity, supported interfaces, capabilities, security requirements, default input and output media types, and skills.
    
    `
    
    {
    
        "name": "Research Agent",
    
        "description": "Finds public sources and returns cited summaries.",
    
        "version": "1.0.0",
    
        "supportedInterfaces": [{
The concrete outputs of a task are Artifacts. The spec recommends returning task outputs as artifacts rather than relying on transient status messages.

Tasks can be short request/response operations or long-running work. Clients can poll with Get Task, stream task updates, subscribe to a task, or configure push notifications when the Agent Card declares those capabilities. Clients must not assume every status message is persisted in task history.

### Bindings, auth, and versioning​

A2A standard bindings are JSON-RPC, gRPC, and HTTP+JSON/REST. The REST binding uses `application/a2a+json`, endpoints such as `POST /message:send`, `POST /message:stream`, and task URLs such as `GET /tasks/{id}`. Streaming uses Server-Sent Events. Agents declare all supported interfaces in `AgentCard.supportedInterfaces`, and all supported bindings must provide equivalent functionality.

Authentication is outside the message body and follows standard web practice. Agent Cards declare `securitySchemes` and `securityRequirements`; requests carry credentials in binding-appropriate headers or metadata. Production A2A must use encrypted transports, validate authorization for every task operation, limit task lists to the caller's access boundary, and avoid logging credentials or personal data. Clients send `A2A-Version` as a header or service parameter; version values use `Major.Minor`, such as `1.0`.

### A2A and MCP

### MCP

⊞

Agent to tool. An agent reaches a server to call a tool or read a resource.

### A2A

⬡

Agent to agent. Two independent agents discover each other, delegate a task, and exchange artifacts.

They are not competitors and a system usually runs both: A2A across the agent graph, MCP down from each agent to its tools. Both are now Linux Foundation projects. The A2A documentation states the two are 'highly complementary' and 'designed to work together'.

#### MCP moved — 2026-07-28

The spec identifies itself by date — the version string is "2026-07-28". The official C# SDK calls its implementation v2.0 and much of the coverage calls it MCP 2; the specification does not. It is billed as the largest revision of the protocol since it launched.

  * Stateless core — from a bidirectional stateful protocol to request/response. Requests are self-describing and can land on any instance behind a load balancer.
  * An Extensions framework, with Tasks moved out of experimental core into the io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks extension (poll-based retrieval and update).

# A2A Protocol: What It Is, Who Ships It and How It Differs From MCP

The A2A protocol is at version 1.0, and most descriptions of it still read like 2025. Version 1.0.0 of the specification is a breaking release: it removes the `kind` discriminator, unifies the Part types and moves errors to `google.rpc.Status`. It defines three protocol bindings, JSON-RPC, gRPC and HTTP+JSON/REST, where Google’s AI Overview names only JSON-RPC. On 27 August 2026 the project was accepted at the Agentic AI Foundation, which sits next to MCP. And four of the six agent frameworks that ship an optional A2A extra on PyPI still cap the A2A SDK below 1.0. We read the specification site, GitHub, PyPI and npm on 2026-10-21 and ran no A2A agent, so this page says nothing about whether any of it interoperates.

Our methodology says how we treat evidence. The script, its raw output and the saved Google AI Overview are in the evidence directory of our public harness repository, and two runs of the script produced byte-identical output.

## What is the A2A protocol?

A2A, short for Agent2Agent, is an open protocol for agents built on different frameworks or by different vendors to find each other and hand work over. An agent publishes an agent card describing what it can do and where to reach it; another agent sends it a task, and the task moves through a lifecycle that can be synchronous, streamed or long-running. Its own announcement describes it as “the horizontal protocol enabling peer-to-peer collaboration”, where MCP is “the vertical integration layer connecting agents to internal tools and databases”.

It is Apache-2.0 licensed. The specification repository, `a2aproject/A2A`, was created on 2025-03-25, is not archived, and had a commit on 2026-10-20. The old `google/A2A` address resolves to the same repository. The latest stable release is v1.0.1 (2026-05-28); the one before it, v1.0.0, was tagged in March 2026 and v0.3.0 in July 2025.

## What changed in A2A version 1.0?

A lot, and some of it breaks code. The specification site lists the latest released version as 1.0.0 and previous versions 0.3.0, 0.2.6 and 0.1.0. Its “What’s New in v1.0” page has a section called “Breaking Changes Requiring Code Updates”, marks Part type unification as “CRITICAL IMPACT”, and rates the stream-event discriminator, the agent-card structure, changed enum values and standardised errors via `google.rpc.Status` as “HIGH IMPACT” and pagination as “MEDIUM IMPACT”. It adds agent-card signing with JSON Web Signatures, and a version header: clients send `A2A-Version`, and a server that does not support the requested version returns an error listing what it does support. We did not test any of this against a running agent.

## Which protocols does A2A run over?

Three. The specification has a section for each: “JSON-RPC Protocol Binding”, “gRPC Protocol Binding” and “HTTP+JSON/REST Protocol Binding”, and says the protocol “supports multiple protocol bindings”, with a section on functional equivalence between them. Google’s AI Overview lists “HTTP(S), JSON-RPC 2.0, Server-Sent Events (SSE), and JSON”. The word gRPC appears 47 times in the specification and not once in the Overview, which also does not name the REST binding. For security, the specification mentions OAuth 44 times, OpenID 3 times, mTLS once and JSON Web Signature 5 times, which is consistent with the Overview’s “TLS, JWTs, and OpenID Connect” but not the whole picture.

## Who governs A2A now?

The Agentic AI Foundation. Its announcement, dated 27 August 2026, says A2A “has officially been accepted as a Growth Stage project at the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF)”, operating “under the Linux Foundation-directed AAIF alongside sibling projects like MCP, goose, and AGENTS.md”. The specification site’s footer reads “Copyright 2026 The Linux Foundation”. Google’s AI Overview says A2A is “governed by the Linux Foundation”, which is accurate but does not mention the foundation or that MCP is a sibling project. The announcement also says the protocol is “backed by over 150 organizations”, which is the project’s own figure and we did not verify it.

# MCP vs A2A: what is the difference?

MCP gives an agent tools to call, and A2A gives it other agents to talk to.

By
    Dan Flanagan

Updated
    October 15, 2026

Checked against
    the MCP specification (modelcontextprotocol.io, protocol version 2026-07-28) and the A2A specification (a2a-protocol.org, version 1.0.0), October 2026

Reading time
    6 min

MCP (Model Context Protocol) connects one agent to the tools and data it needs: a database, a calendar, a ticketing system. A2A (Agent2Agent) connects that agent to a different, independent agent, one it does not control and whose internals it never sees. Both are open specifications, and a system can use both.

## What each protocol is for

MCP's specification describes a host (the AI application), a client inside it, and a server that exposes tools, resources and prompts. A client calls `tools/list` to learn what a server offers, then `tools/call` to run one. The server does the work and returns a result. Nothing in that exchange assumes the thing on the other end is itself an agent.

Establish governed MCP and A2A connections by routing clients through the Agent Gateway, which manages identity, policy enforcement, and observability before forwarding requests to your local servers or cloud-deployed agents (e.g., Vertex AI Agent Engine).

## Protocol Support

The labs exercise the following Agent Gateway protocol versions:

Protocol  | Wire-protocol version  | Lab  | Notes

MCP  | `2024-11-05`  | `mcp/`  | Initialization-based MCP flow
MCP  | `2026-07-28`  | `mcp-latest/`  | Stateless modern MCP flow with per-request metadata and `server/discover`

> `1.0.1` is the A2A Python SDK release used by the v1 lab; the A2A wire protocol advertised in the agent card and request header is `1.0`.

###### CORRECTLY RETURNING 404

All expected 404 endpoints confirmed:

  * /api — 404
  * /health — 404
  * /.well-known/agent.json — 404
  * /.well-known/agents.json — 404
  * /.well-known/agents.txt — 404
  * /.well-known/llms.txt — 404

##### Performance Analysis

**Response Times:**

  * Fastest: /agents.json (609ms)
  * Average: Most endpoints 700-900ms
  * Slowest: /api/v1/metrics (3401ms), /openapi.json (3094ms)
  * **Concern:** Metrics and OpenAPI are 3-5x slower than other endpoints

**Intermittency:**

  * **NONE DETECTED** - Tested /api/v1/capabilities 3 times, all returned consistent 200 status
  * Response times varied (954ms, 1775ms, 1047ms) but all successful
  * Content size identical (18951 bytes) - no cache invalidation issues

##### Detailed Findings

###### 1. A2A Agent Card Status: OPERATIONAL

The report that /.well-known/agent-card.json was failing appears to be **incorrect or time-sensitive**. My test shows:

  * Status: 200
  * Content-Type: application/a2a+json; charset=utf-8
  * Size: 2371 bytes
  * Parseable: true
  * Skills: 3

The card correctly uses application/a2a+json content type (not generic application/json), which is A2A v1.0 compliant.

**Possible explanation for earlier failures:**

  * Temporary DNS/CDN propagation delay
  * Cloudflare edge caching issue (now resolved)
  * Rate limiting that has since expired

###### 2. MCP Endpoint: FUNCTIONAL but STRICT

The MCP endpoint is working correctly per the 2026-07-28 specification.

**Test performed:**

  * POST /mcp with header MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28
  * Body with jsonrpc 2.0 and tools/call method

**Result:** HTTP 400 with JSON-RPC error code -32020

**Analysis:** This is CORRECT behavior. The MCP 2026-07-28 spec requires protocol version in BOTH:

1. HTTP header: MCP-Protocol-Version: 2026-07-28

2. Request body: params._meta.io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion: 2026-07-28

The error message is clear and actionable. This is not a bug - it is spec compliance.

### The v0.3 → v1.0 breaking changes

If you built against A2A in 2025, this list is your migration plan:

v0.3.0  | v1.0
--- | ---
`message/send`  | `SendMessage`
`message/stream`  | `SendStreamingMessage`
`tasks/get`  | `GetTask`
`tasks/cancel`  | `CancelTask`
`tasks/resubscribe`  | `SubscribeToTask`
`agent/getAuthenticatedExtendedCard`  | `GetExtendedAgentCard`
—  | `ListTasks` (new, cursor-paginated)
`preferredTransport` + `additionalInterfaces`  | `supportedInterfaces[]`
`protocolVersion` on the card  | per-interface `protocolVersion`
`kind` discriminator fields  | removed — discriminate on JSON member names
kebab-case enums (`input-required`)  | SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE (`TASK_STATE_INPUT_REQUIRED`)
compound IDs (`tasks/{id}/…`)  | flat UUIDs
`POST /v1/message:send`  | `POST /message:send` (no `/v1` prefix)
implicit + password OAuth flows  | removed; Device Code (RFC 8628) added; `pkce_required` added

Also new in v1.0: a `tenant` field on every request (multi-tenancy without URL gymnastics), and a mandatory version header:
    
    `POST /a2a HTTP/1.1
    Host: api.sharksapi.ai
    A2A-Version: 1.0
    Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs...
    Content-Type: application/json
    `

An empty `A2A-Version` header is interpreted as `0.3`. If you forget it, you silently get old semantics. Send it.

### Delegating a task
    
    `{
      "jsonrpc": "2.0",
      "id": "req-01",
      "method": "SendMessage",
      "params": {
        "message": {
          "role": "user",
          "messageId": "c1f9a2e0-6b34-4f1a-9a7e-2f0d3b8c4a11",
          "parts": [
            { "text": "Audit example.ee and return the top 10 crawl blockers." }
          ]
        },
        "configuration": {
          "returnImmediately": true,
          "acceptedOutputModes": ["application/json"]
        }
      }
    }
    `

With `returnImmediately: true` you get a `Task` back straight away, in `TASK_STATE_SUBMITTED` or `TASK_STATE_WORKING`, and you then poll `GetTask`, open a `SubscribeToTask` SSE stream, or register a webhook via `CreateTaskPushNotificationConfig`.
